# Peer review - Round 1

Reviewers:
- Anonymous Reviewer

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100525.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100525.3.sa1)

Summary:

How reconsolidation works - particularly in humans - remains largely unknown. With an elegant, 3-day design, combining fMRI and psychopharmacology, the authors provide evidence for a certain role for noradrenaline in the reconsolidation of memory for neutral stimuli. All memory tasks were performed in the context of fMRI scanning, with additional resting state acquisitions performed before and after recall testing on Day 2. On Day 1, 3 groups of healthy participants encoded word-picture associates (with pictures being either scenes or objects) and then performed an immediate cued recall task to presentation of the word (answering is the word old or new, and was it paired with a scene or an object). On Day 2, the cued recall task was repeated using half of the stimulus set words encoded on Day 1 (only old words were presented, with subjects required to indicate prior scene vs object pairing). This test was immediately preceded by the oral administration of placebo, cortisol, or yohimibine (to raise noradrenaline levels) depending on group assignment. On Day 3, all words presented on Day 1 were presented. As expected, on Day 3, memory was significantly enhanced for associations that were cued and successfully retrieved on Day 2 compared to uncued associations. However, for associative d', there was no Cued × Group interaction nor a main effect of Group, i.e., on the standard measure of memory performance, post-retrieval drug presence on Day 2 did not affect memory reconsolidation. As further evidence for a null result, fMRI univariate analyses showed no Cued × Group interactions in whole-brain or ROI activity.

Strengths:

There are some aspects of this study that I find impressive. The study is well-designed and the fMRI analysis methodology innovative and sound. The authors have made meticulous and thorough physiological measurements, and assays of mood, throughout the experiment. By doing so, they have overcome, to a considerable extent, the difficulties inherent in timing of human oral drug delivery in reconsolidation tasks, where it is difficult to have drug present in the immediate recall period without affecting recall itself. This is beautifully shown in Fig. 3. I also think that having some neurobiological assay of memory reactivation when studying reconsolidation in humans is critical, and the authors provide this. While multi-voxel patterns of hemodynamic responses are, in my view, very difficult to equate with an "engram", these patterns do have something to do with memory.

Weaknesses:

I have major issues regarding the behavioral results and the framing of the manuscript:

(1) To arrive at group differences in memory performance, the authors performed median splitting of Day 3 trials by short and long reaction times during memory cueing on Day 2, as they took this as a putative measure of high/low levels of memory reactivation. Associative category hits on Day 3 showed a Group by Day 2 Reaction time (short, long) interaction, with post-hocs showing (according to the text) worse memory for short Day 2 RTs in the yohimbine group. These post-hocs should be corrected for multiple comparisons, as the result is not what would be predicted (see point 2). My primary issue here is that we are not given RT data for each group, nor is the median splitting procedure described in the methods. Was this across all groups, or within groups? Are short RTs in the yohimbine group any different from short RTs in the other two groups? Unfortunately, we are not given Day 2 picture category memory levels or reaction times for each group. This is relevant because (as given in Supplemental Table S1) memory performance (d´) for the Yohimbine group on Day 1 immediate testing is (roughly speaking) 20% lower than the other 2 groups (independently of whether the pairs will be presented again the following day). I appreciate that this is not significant in a group x performance ANOVA but how does this relate to later memory performance? What were the group-specific RTs on Day 1? So, before the reader goes into the fMRI results, there are questions regarding the supposed drug-induced changes in behavior. Indeed, in the discussion, there is repeated mention of subsequent memory impairment produced by yohimbine but the nature of the impairment is not clear.

This weakness was satisfactorily addressed in one revision round. As RT data are often not normally distributed, were they transformed prior to entry into linear models?

(2) The authors should be clearer as to what their original hypotheses were, and why they did the experiment. Despite being a complex literature, I would have thought the hypotheses would be reconsolidation impairment by cortisol and enhancement by yohimbine. Here it is relevant to point out that - only when the reader gets to the Methods section - there is mention of a paper published by this group in 2024. In this publication, the authors used the same study design but administered a stress manipulation after Day 2 cued recall, instead of a pharmacological one. They did not find a difference in associative hit rate between stress and control groups, but - similar to the current manuscript - reported that post-retrieval stress disrupts subsequent remembering (Day 3 performance) depending on neural memory reinstatement during reactivation (specifically driven by the hippocampus and its correlation with neocortical areas).

Instead of using these results, and other human studies, to motivate the current work, reference is made to a recent animal study: Line 169 "Building on recent findings in rodents (Khalaf et al. 2018), we hypothesized that the effects of post-retrieval noradrenergic and glucocorticoid activation would critically depend on the reinstatement of the neural event representation during retrieval". It is difficult to follow that a rodent study using contextual fear conditioning and examining single neuron activity to remote fear recall and extinction would be relevant enough to motivate a hypothesis for a human psychopharmacological study on emotionally neutral paired associates.

Minor comments

- Related to Major issue 2. In the introduction, it would be helpful to be specific about the type of memory being probed in the different studies referenced (episodic vs conditioning). For the former, please make it clear whether stimuli to be remembered were emotional or neutral, and for which stimulus class drug effects were observed. This is particularly important given that in the first paragraph you describe memory reactivation in the context of traumatic memories via mention of PTSD. It would also be helpful to know to which species you refer. For example, in line 115, "timing of drug administration..." a rodent and a human study are cited.

This weakness was addressed in one revision round, resulting in an excellent introduction, highlighting the importance of studying post-retrieval effects for memory researchers and healthcare workers.

claims.source: However, rodent studies on neutral recognition memory (Maroun and Akirav, 2008), fear conditioning (Vafaei et al., 2023), as well as evidence from humans on episodic recognition memory (Antypa et al., 2021) report impairing effects of glucocorticoid receptor activation on post-retrieval memory dynamics.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent and human studies.

claims.claim: Post-retrieval blockade of noradrenergic activity impairs putative reconsolidation or future memory accessibility in human fear conditioning.
claims.source: For noradrenaline, post-retrieval blockade of noradrenergic activity impairs putative reconsolidation or future memory accessibility in human fear conditioning (Kindt et al., 2009), as well as drug (alcohol) memory (Schramm et al., 2016) and spatial memory in rodents (Przybyslawski et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human and rodent studies.

claims.claim: The effect of noradrenergic blockade on memory is not consistently observed in human studies on fear conditioning, speaking anxiety, inhibitory avoidance, and traumatic mental imagination.
claims.source: However, this effect is not consistently observed in human studies on fear conditioning (Bos et al., 2014a), speaking anxiety (Elsey et al., 2020), inhibitory avoidance (Muravieva and Alberini, 2010), traumatic mental imagination (PTSD patients) (Wood et al., 2015), and might depend on the arousal state of the individual (Maroun and Akirav, 2008) or the exact timing of drug administration as suggested by studies in humans (Thomas et al., 2017) and rodents (Otis et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing inconsistent effects.

claims.claim: Brain regions implicated in initial memory formation, such as the hippocampus, may also play a role in the modification of memories after their reactivation.
claims.source: Extant studies suggest that brain regions implicated in initial memory formation, such as the hippocampus, may also play a role in the modification of memories after their reactivation (Nader et al., 2000; Przybyslawski and Sara, 1997; Schwabe et al., 2012b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Research in transgenic mice indicates that effective post-reactivation interventions require the reactivation of specific neuronal subsets within the engram.
claims.source: Research in transgenic mice indicates that effective post-reactivation interventions require the reactivation of specific neuronal subsets within the engram, underscoring the significant contribution of the original memory trace to changes during the proposed reconsolidation window (Khalaf et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a mouse study.

claims.claim: Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) enables the assessment of neural pattern reinstatement at the stimulus category or event level in humans.
claims.source: While human neuroimaging studies cannot assess the reactivation of individual neurons within an engram, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) enables the assessment of neural pattern reinstatement at the stimulus category or event level (Staresina et al., 2012; Wing et al., 2015; Thakral et al., 2015; Polyn et al., 2005; Kuhl et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to MVPA methodology papers.

claims.claim: Memory reactivation occurs not only during goal-directed retrieval (online) but also offline during post-retrieval rest periods.
claims.source: Notably, memory reactivation occurs not only during goal-directed retrieval (online) but also offline during post-retrieval rest periods.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about memory processes based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Online reactivation reflects the immediate impact of memory retrieval on neural networks and may involve modifications of the existing memory trace and/or the encoding of a new memory trace in response to retrieval demands.
claims.source: Online reactivation reflects the immediate impact of memory retrieval on neural networks and may involve modifications of the existing memory trace and/or the encoding of a new memory trace in response to retrieval demands (Tanaka et al., 2014; Johnson and Rugg, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Offline reactivation offers a pivotal window for the consolidation and stabilization of memory alterations.
claims.source: Offline reactivation offers a pivotal window for the consolidation and stabilization of these memory alterations (Tambini et al., 2010; Oudiette and Paller, 2013; Staresina et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The transition from online to offline reactivation involves complex neural cascades, influencing the persistence and strength of the reactivated memory trace.
claims.source: The transition from online to offline reactivation involves complex neural cascades, influencing the persistence and strength of the reactivated memory trace (Yagi et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Participants successfully distinguished between old words and new words on Day 1, with a 74.4% hit rate and a 16.8% false alarm rate.
claims.source: Participants successfully distinguished between old words and new words, with a 74.4% hit rate (response 'old,' 'old/scene,' 'old/object' to an old word) and a 16.8% false alarm rate (response 'old,' 'old/scene,' 'old/object' to a new word).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the Day 1 immediate cued recall task.

claims.claim: Participants recognized the word and correctly identified the associated image category in 47.3% of trials on Day 1.
claims.source: Participants recognized the word and correctly identified the associated image category in 47.3% of trials (associative category hit rate) with an associative error rate of 13.1%.
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the Day 1 immediate cued recall task.

claims.claim: The average associative d' on Day 1 was 1.13.
claims.source: Signal detection theory-based analysis revealed an average associative d' of 1.13 (SE = 0.09).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the Day 1 immediate cued recall task.

claims.claim: Immediate cued recall performance on Day 1 did not differ between pairs later cued and uncued on Day 2.
claims.source: Because the critical stress system manipulations were implemented only on Day 2 (hydrocortisone, yohimbine, placebo groups), we confirmed that immediate cued recall performance on Day 1 did not differ between pairs later cued and uncued on Day 2 (F(1,58) = 1.25, p=0.267, η2<0.01), nor between groups (all main or interaction effects; all Ps>0.481; see Appendix 1—table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result confirming no baseline differences between conditions.

claims.claim: Groups did not differ in mood, arousal, or cortisol levels before encoding on Day 1.
claims.source: Moreover, groups did not differ in mood, arousal, or cortisol levels before encoding on Day 1 (all Ps>0.564; see Appendix 1—table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result confirming no baseline differences between groups.

claims.claim: Whole-brain fMRI analyses on immediate cued recall data revealed no significant main or interaction effects involving Group.
claims.source: Whole-brain fMRI analyses on immediate cued recall data (associative category hits >associative misses), considering the within-subject factor Cued and the between-subjects factor Group, revealed no significant main or interaction effects (all Ps>0.564; see Appendix 1—table 2).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI result showing no group differences on Day 1.

claims.claim: Before the Memory Cueing task on Day 2, there were no significant differences between groups in subjective mood, autonomic arousal, or salivary cortisol.
claims.source: Before the Memory Cueing task, there were no significant differences between groups in subjective mood, autonomic arousal, or salivary cortisol (all Ps>0.096, Appendix 1—table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result confirming no baseline differences before drug administration.

claims.claim: During the Memory Cueing task on Day 2, participants accurately identified the correct picture category in 67.5% of trials.
claims.source: Overall, participants performed well, accurately identifying the correct picture category in 67.5% of trials (SE = 2.6%; chance = 50%), and the three groups did not differ in performance (F(2,58) = 1.53, p=0.224, η2=0.05; see Appendix 1—table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the Day 2 Memory Cueing task.

claims.claim: The three groups did not differ in performance during the Memory Cueing task on Day 2.
claims.source: Overall, participants performed well, accurately identifying the correct picture category in 67.5% of trials (SE = 2.6%; chance = 50%), and the three groups did not differ in performance (F(2,58) = 1.53, p=0.224, η2=0.05; see Appendix 1—table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group differences in Day 2 performance.

claims.claim: A whole-brain fMRI analysis revealed significant activation in bilateral hippocampi during successful memory retrieval on Day 2.
claims.source: A whole-brain fMRI analysis revealed significant activation in bilateral hippocampi (Left: [-26,–32, –10], t=7.93, P(FWE)<0.001; Right: [32, -40, -12], t=7.89, P(FWE)<0.001), ventral temporal cortex (VTC; Left: [-30,–40, –12], t=7.75, P(FWE)<0.001; Right: [52, -50, -14], t=7.26, P(FWE)<0.001), and PCC ([4, -42, 38], t=8.10, P(FWE)<0.001), along with other regions central for episodic memory retrieval (e.g. medial prefrontal cortex; see Appendix 1—table 3).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI result showing brain activation during successful retrieval.

claims.claim: A whole-brain fMRI analysis revealed significant activation in ventral temporal cortex (VTC) during successful memory retrieval on Day 2.
claims.source: A whole-brain fMRI analysis revealed significant activation in bilateral hippocampi (Left: [-26,–32, –10], t=7.93, P(FWE)<0.001; Right: [32, -40, -12], t=7.89, P(FWE)<0.001), ventral temporal cortex (VTC; Left: [-30,–40, –12], t=7.75, P(FWE)<0.001; Right: [52, -50, -14], t=7.26, P(FWE)<0.001), and PCC ([4, -42, 38], t=8.10, P(FWE)<0.001), along with other regions central for episodic memory retrieval (e.g. medial prefrontal cortex; see Appendix 1—table 3).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI result showing brain activation during successful retrieval.

claims.claim: A whole-brain fMRI analysis revealed significant activation in PCC during successful memory retrieval on Day 2.
claims.source: A whole-brain fMRI analysis revealed significant activation in bilateral hippocampi (Left: [-26,–32, –10], t=7.93, P(FWE)<0.001; Right: [32, -40, -12], t=7.89, P(FWE)<0.001), ventral temporal cortex (VTC; Left: [-30,–40, –12], t=7.75, P(FWE)<0.001; Right: [52, -50, -14], t=7.26, P(FWE)<0.001), and PCC ([4, -42, 38], t=8.10, P(FWE)<0.001), along with other regions central for episodic memory retrieval (e.g. medial prefrontal cortex; see Appendix 1—table 3).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI result showing brain activation during successful retrieval.

claims.claim: There were no group differences in univariate brain activity related to successful retrieval during the Memory Cueing task.
claims.source: Importantly, there were no group differences in univariate brain activity related to successful retrieval during the Memory Cueing task (all Retrieval success × Group interaction Ps >0.420).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group differences in brain activity during Day 2.

claims.claim: Higher hippocampal activity was associated with faster 2AFC reaction times during Day 2 Memory Cueing.
claims.source: A linear mixed-effects model (LMM) using participants' reaction times as a proxy for memory confidence/memory strength revealed that higher hippocampal as well as PCC activity was associated with faster 2AFC reaction times (Left hippocampus: β=–0.51 ± 0.18, t=–2.88, PCorr = 0.018, R2conditional = 0.08; Right hippocampus: β=–0.47 ± 0.18, t=–2.60, PCorr = 0.033, R2conditional = 0.11; PCC: β=–0.75 ± 0.20, t=–3.67, PCorr <0.001, R2conditional = 0.09), while no such relation was observed in the VTC (PCorr = 0.282).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed-effects modeling.

claims.claim: Higher PCC activity was associated with faster 2AFC reaction times during Day 2 Memory Cueing.
claims.source: A linear mixed-effects model (LMM) using participants' reaction times as a proxy for memory confidence/memory strength revealed that higher hippocampal as well as PCC activity was associated with faster 2AFC reaction times (Left hippocampus: β=–0.51 ± 0.18, t=–2.88, PCorr = 0.018, R2conditional = 0.08; Right hippocampus: β=–0.47 ± 0.18, t=–2.60, PCorr = 0.033, R2conditional = 0.11; PCC: β=–0.75 ± 0.20, t=–3.67, PCorr <0.001, R2conditional = 0.09), while no such relation was observed in the VTC (PCorr = 0.282).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed-effects modeling.

claims.claim: No relation was observed between VTC activity and reaction times during Day 2 Memory Cueing.
claims.source: A linear mixed-effects model (LMM) using participants' reaction times as a proxy for memory confidence/memory strength revealed that higher hippocampal as well as PCC activity was associated with faster 2AFC reaction times (Left hippocampus: β=–0.51 ± 0.18, t=–2.88, PCorr = 0.018, R2conditional = 0.08; Right hippocampus: β=–0.47 ± 0.18, t=–2.60, PCorr = 0.033, R2conditional = 0.11; PCC: β=–0.75 ± 0.20, t=–3.67, PCorr <0.001, R2conditional = 0.09), while no such relation was observed in the VTC (PCorr = 0.282).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed-effects modeling.

claims.claim: The average classifier accuracy for scene vs. object discrimination in VTC was 90.0%.
claims.source: For the VTC, the average classifier accuracy was high (M ± SD: 90.0% ± 0.1%); t(60) = 25.99, PCorr <0.001, d=3.83 indicative of reliable category-level processing in the VTC.
claims.evidence: This is a result from MVPA classification analysis on the localizer task.

claims.claim: There were no significant group differences in VTC classification accuracy during the localizer task.
claims.source: Importantly, there were no significant group differences in classification accuracy (F(1,59) = 2.56, PCorr = 0.115, η2=0.04).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group differences in classifier performance.

claims.claim: The localizer-trained classifier achieved 77.9% accuracy when tested on Day 1 Encoding task data.
claims.source: Further probing VTC category processing, we next tested the localizer-trained classifier on the Day 1 Encoding task (Figure 2B), in which objects and scenes were presented. Average accuracy was again high (M ± SD: 77.9% ± 0.9%, t(60) = 29.88, PCorr <0.001, d=3.80), further supporting category-level processing in the VTC, again without significant group differences in classification accuracy (F(2,58) = 0.44, PCorr = 0.643, η2=0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MVPA classification analysis testing generalization to encoding data, with reference to Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Associative hits during Day 2 Memory Cueing were accompanied by stronger visual category pattern reinstatement in VTC, compared to associative misses.
claims.source: Using the localizer-trained logistic classifier, testing on all trials of the Memory Cueing task (in which only words but not associated images were presented) confirmed that associative hits were accompanied by stronger visual category pattern reinstatement in VTC, compared to associative misses (main effect Retrieval Success: F(1,58) = 12.45, PCorr <0.001, η2=0.13).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MVPA analysis showing category reinstatement during retrieval.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences between groups in VTC reinstatement during the Memory Cueing task.
claims.source: Importantly, there were no significant differences between groups in VTC reinstatement during the Memory Cueing task (all main and interaction effects, Ps >0.504).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group differences in VTC reinstatement.

claims.claim: Successful memory cueing on Day 2 was associated with greater trial-wise category-level reinstatement in the VTC.
claims.source: A generalized linear mixed model revealed a main effect of Retrieval success (F(1,58) = 12.61, PCorr = 0.003, η2=0.13), but no effect of Group and no Group ×Retrieval success interaction (both Ps = 1), showing that successful memory cueing on Day 2 was associated with greater trial-wise category-level reinstatement in the VTC, without differences between groups.
claims.evidence: This is a result from generalized linear mixed model analysis.

claims.claim: The classifier distinguished remembered scenes from remembered objects during the Memory Cueing task, performing significantly above chance-level (54.4%).
claims.source: Finally, we tested the VTC-trained classifier selectively on associative hit trials, corresponding to remembered scenes and objects, during the Memory Cueing task. Overall, the classifier distinguished remembered scenes from remembered objects, performing significantly above chance-level (50%; M ± SE = 54.4% ± 1.0%; t(60) = 4.44, PCorr <0.001, d=1.14), without a difference between scenes and objects (p=0.092).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MVPA classification analysis on remembered trials.

claims.claim: When tested on associative miss trials, the classifier failed to differentiate forgotten scenes from forgotten objects.
claims.source: By contrast, when tested on associative miss trials, the classifier failed to differentiate forgotten scenes from forgotten objects (M ± SE = 50.1% ± 1.7%; PCorr = 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MVPA classification analysis on forgotten trials.

claims.claim: Classifier accuracy on remembered trials in VTC did not differ between groups.
claims.source: Again, classifier accuracy on remembered trials in VTC did not differ between groups (F(2,58) = 0.86, PCorr = 1, η2=0.03).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group differences in classifier performance.

claims.claim: The average accuracy scores for scene vs. object classification in the hippocampus using localizer data did not significantly differ from chance.
claims.source: We also examined scene vs. object classification accuracy in the left and right hippocampus, using data from the independent localizer. The average accuracy scores did not significantly differ from chance (50%; Left: M ± SD: 53.3% ± 1.8%, t(60) = 1.72, PCorr = 0.501, d=0.22; Right: M ± SD: 52.9% ± 1.5%, t(60) = 1.50, PCorr = 0.520, d=0.18), indicating poor category-coding in the hippocampus (Liang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MVPA classification analysis showing poor category discrimination in hippocampus.

claims.claim: The hippocampus shows poor category-coding.
claims.source: The average accuracy scores did not significantly differ from chance (50%; Left: M ± SD: 53.3% ± 1.8%, t(60) = 1.72, PCorr = 0.501, d=0.22; Right: M ± SD: 52.9% ± 1.5%, t(60) = 1.50, PCorr = 0.520, d=0.18), indicating poor category-coding in the hippocampus (Liang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on classification results and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Classifiers trained on localizer activation patterns in the hippocampus were not able to distinguish remembered scenes from remembered objects during Day 2 Memory Cueing.
claims.source: However, in contrast to VTC, classifiers trained on localizer activation patterns in the left and right hippocampus were neither able to distinguish remembered scenes and remembered objects (Left: M ± SE = 50.71% ± 1.0%; t(60) = 0.69, PCorr = 1, d=0.09; Right: M ± SE = 51.82% ± 0.9%; t(60) = 2.10, PCorr = 0.156, d=0.23), nor forgotten scenes and forgotten objects (Left: M ± SE = 47.95% ± 1.6%; t(60) = –1.31, PCorr = 1, d=0.17; Right: M ± SE = 49.61% ± 1.3%; t(60) = –0.27, PCorr = 1, d=0.09) when tested on Day 2 Memory Cueing task data.
claims.evidence: This is a result from MVPA classification analysis showing no category discrimination in hippocampus during retrieval.

claims.claim: The average accuracy scores for scene vs. object classification in the PCC using localizer data significantly exceeded chance level (62.4%).
claims.source: Finally, we examined scene vs. object classification accuracy in the PCC using localizer task data. The average accuracy scores significantly exceeded chance level (50%; M ± SD: 62.4% ± 2.24%, t(60) = 5.39, PCorr <0.001, d=0.69), indicating category-coding in PCC, without group differences (F(1,59) = 0.81, PCorr = 0.370, η2=0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MVPA classification analysis showing category discrimination in PCC.

claims.claim: The classifier trained on PCC localizer patterns was not able to distinguish remembered scenes from remembered objects during the Day 2 Memory Cueing task.
claims.source: The classifier trained on localizer activation patterns in the PCC was neither able to distinguish remembered scenes and remembered objects during the Day 2 Memory Cueing task (M ± SE = 52.3% ± 0.98%; PCorr = 0.092), nor forgotten scenes and forgotten objects (M ± SE = 49.5% ± 1.70%; t(60) = –0.27, PCorr = 1, d=0.03).
claims.evidence: This is a result from MVPA classification analysis showing no category discrimination in PCC during retrieval.

claims.claim: Within-localizer classifier accuracies revealed significantly higher accuracy for the VTC compared to PCC and hippocampus.
claims.source: Contrasting within-localizer classifier accuracies revealed a main-effect of Region (F(2,174) = 101.74, PCorr <0.001, η2=0.054). Post-hoc tests revealed significantly higher accuracy for the VTC compared to PCC (t(60) = –12.00, PCorr <0.001, d=1.54) and hippocampus (t(60) = –17.40, p<0.001, d=2.24), and for the PCC compared to the hippocampus (t(60) = –3.90, PCorr <0.001, d=0.50).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison of classifier accuracies across regions.

claims.claim: Category-level reinstatement during Day 1 Encoding was found in the VTC, PCC, and hippocampus, with significantly higher accuracy for the VTC compared to PCC and hippocampus.
claims.source: Moreover, while we found evidence for category-level reinstatement during Day 1 Encoding in the VTC, PCC, and hippocampus, a main-effect of Region (F(2,174) = 192.32, p<.001, η2=0.69) revealed significantly higher accuracy for the VTC compared to PCC (t(60) = –16.90, PCorr <0.001, d=2.18) and hippocampus (t(60) = –19.01, PCorr <0.001, d=2.45).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison of classifier accuracies across regions during encoding.

claims.claim: Classifier accuracy of PCC and hippocampus did not differ during the Encoding task.
claims.source: Classifier accuracy of PCC and hippocampus did not differ during the Encoding task (t(60) = 0.94, PCorr = 1, d=0.12).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison showing no difference between PCC and hippocampus.

claims.claim: Significant category-level reinstatement of remembered trials during the Day 2 Memory Cueing task was observed in cortical areas (VTC, PCC), but not in the hippocampus.
claims.source: Finally, significant category-level reinstatement of remembered trials during the Day 2 Memory Cueing task was observed in cortical areas (VTC, PCC), but not in the hippocampus.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of MVPA results comparing regions during retrieval.

claims.claim: VTC accuracy was significantly higher than hippocampal accuracy during Day 2 Memory Cueing.
claims.source: Comparing corresponding accuracy estimates revealed a main-effect of Region (F(2,174) = 3.45, p=0.034, η2=0.04). Post-hoc tests showed no difference between VTC and PCC (t(60) = –1.69, PCorr = 0.283, d=0.22) nor PCC and hippocampus (t(60) = 1.24, PCorr = 0.660, d=0.16), whereas VTC accuracy was significantly higher than hippocampal accuracy (t(60) = –2.61, PCorr = 0.034, d=0.34).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison of classifier accuracies across regions during retrieval.

claims.claim: In PCC and hippocampus, there was no evidence for event-level memory trace reinstatement from Day 1 to Day 2.
claims.source: To test for evidence that associative hits during memory cueing entailed the reinstatement of representations established at encoding, we compared the average event-level Day 1 (encoding) to Day 2 (memory cueing) similarity of the associative hits against 0. In PCC and hippocampus, we did not obtain evidence for event-level memory trace reinstatement (t-test against 0; both PCorr >0.296).
claims.evidence: This is a result from RSA analysis showing no event-level reinstatement.

claims.claim: For the VTC, average similarity from Day 1 to Day 2 was significantly negative, suggesting that neural patterns became more dissimilar.
claims.source: By contrast, for the VTC, average similarity was significantly negative, suggesting that from Day 1 (encoding) to Day 2 (memory cueing), neural patterns became more dissimilar (t(60) = –7.87, PCorr <0.001, d=1.01).
claims.evidence: This is a result from RSA analysis showing pattern dissimilarity.

claims.claim: Memory trace reinstatement during successful memory cueing on Day 2 was characterized by significantly higher category-level representations compared to event-level representations in all three regions (hippocampus, VTC, PCC).
claims.source: As the VTC is implicated in category-level processing, we next compared trial-wise event- vs category-level similarities. Results revealed that memory trace reinstatement during successful memory cueing on Day 2 (i.e. associative hits) was characterized by significantly higher category-level representations compared to event-level representations in all three regions (hippocampus: t(60) = 5.51, PCorr <0.001, d=0.71; VTC: t(60) = –11.83, PCorr <0.001, d=1.51; PCC: t(60) = 8.25, PCorr <0.001, d=1.06).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical comparison showing category-level dominance over event-level reinstatement.

claims.claim: Analysis of autonomic measures revealed a significant Time × Group interaction in systolic blood pressure.
claims.source: Analysis of autonomic measures revealed a significant Time × Group interaction in systolic blood pressure (F(8.71, 256.99)=5.87, p<0.001, η2=.03; Figure 3A), but not in diastolic blood pressure or heart rate (both Ps >0.120; Appendix 1—table 6).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from physiological measurements, with reference to Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Systolic blood pressure was significantly higher in the YOH group compared to the PLAC group at 70, 85, and 100 minutes after pill intake.
claims.source: Post-hoc t-tests showed significantly higher systolic blood pressure in the YOH group compared to the PLAC group 70 min (t(29.77)=–3.31, PCorr = 0.014, d=1.02), 85 min (t(34.15)=–3.33, PCorr = 0.012, d=1.03), and 100 min after pill intake (t(36.94)=–3.98, PCorr <0.001, d=1.23).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests on blood pressure data.

claims.claim: The CORT group did not significantly differ from the PLAC group in systolic blood pressure.
claims.source: The CORT group did not significantly differ from the PLAC group in systolic blood pressure (all Ps >0.229).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no difference between CORT and PLAC groups.

claims.claim: Systolic blood pressure in the YOH and CORT groups did not differ from the PLAC group immediately before or after the MRI session.
claims.source: Importantly, systolic blood pressure in the YOH and CORT groups did not differ from the PLAC group immediately before or after the MRI session, suggesting that the drug was not yet effective during the Memory Cueing task and the post-reactivation resting-state scan (both Ps >0.485).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result confirming timing of drug effects.

claims.claim: Skin conductance response analysis during the Memory Cueing task and resting-state scans showed no Time × Group interaction.
claims.source: Skin conductance response analysis during the Memory Cueing task and pre- and post-reactivation resting-state scans showed no Time × Group interaction (F(3.30, 97.44)=0.33, p=0.819, η2<0.01) and no main effect of Group (F(2,59) = 2.60, p=0.083, η2=0.07), suggesting that groups did not reliably differ in autonomic arousal during the MRI scans.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from skin conductance measurements.

claims.claim: Salivary cortisol increased in the CORT group but not in the YOH or PLAC groups.
claims.source: In contrast to systolic blood pressure, salivary cortisol increased, as expected, in the CORT group but not in the YOH or PLAC groups (Time × Group interaction: F(5.33, 157.17)=43.80, p<0.001, η2=0.472).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from salivary cortisol measurements.

claims.claim: Salivary cortisol was significantly higher in the CORT group compared to the PLAC group at 40, 70, and 100 minutes after pill intake.
claims.source: Post-hoc t-tests indicated a significant cortisol increase in the CORT group compared to the PLAC group at 40 min (t(27.91)=2.30, PCorr = 0.020, d=0.99), 70 min (t(20.64)=–11.23, PCorr <0.001, d=3.42), and 100 min after pill intake (t(20.19)=–10.36, p<0.001, d=3.15; Figure 3B), whereas salivary cortisol of PLAC and YOH groups revealed no significant difference at any timepoint (all PCorr >0.350).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests on cortisol data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Salivary cortisol concentrations did not differ between groups immediately before or during the MRI session.
claims.source: Importantly, salivary cortisol concentrations did not differ between groups immediately before or during the MRI session, suggesting that CORT was not yet effective during the Memory Cueing task or post-reactivation resting-state scan (both PCorr >0.162).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result confirming timing of drug effects.

claims.claim: Subjective mood analyses across Day 2 revealed no significant Time × Group interaction on any scale.
claims.source: Finally, subjective mood analyses across Day 2 revealed no significant Time × Group interaction on any scale (all interaction Ps >0.460; Appendix 1—table 7).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from mood questionnaires.

claims.claim: Both hydrocortisone and yohimbine are active within the time window that is critical for potential reconsolidation effects.
claims.source: Our data demonstrate that, despite the distinct pharmacodynamics of CORT and YOH, both substances are active within the time window that is critical for potential reconsolidation effects (Nader and Einarsson, 2010; Lee et al., 2017; Nader et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the physiological data and supported by citations about reconsolidation timing.

claims.claim: Groups did not differ in subjective mood, autonomic arousal, or salivary cortisol before the final memory test on Day 3.
claims.source: On Day 3, 24 hrafter memory cueing and drug administration, participants returned to the MRI scanner for a final cued recall task. Groups did not differ in subjective mood, autonomic arousal, or salivary cortisol before this final memory test (all Ps>0.158, see Appendix 1—table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result confirming no baseline differences on Day 3.

claims.claim: Participants successfully distinguished between old words and new words on Day 3, with an 81.1% hit rate and a 21.75% false alarm rate.
claims.source: Participants successfully distinguished between old words and new words, with an 81.1% hit rate (response 'old,' 'old/scene,' 'old/object' to an old word) and a 21.75% false alarm rate (response 'old,' 'old/scene,' 'old/object' to a new word).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the Day 3 cued recall task.

claims.claim: Participants recognized the word and correctly identified the associated image category in 50.1% of trials on Day 3.
claims.source: Participants recognized the word and correctly identified the associated image category in 50.1% of trials (associative category hit rate) with an associative error rate of 11.6%.
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the Day 3 cued recall task.

claims.claim: Day 3 associative d' was 1.14.
claims.source: Day 3 associative d' was 1.14 (SE = 0.15).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the Day 3 cued recall task.

claims.claim: Memory was significantly enhanced for associations that were cued and successfully retrieved on Day 2 compared to uncued associations.
claims.source: Importantly, across groups, memory was significantly enhanced for associations that were cued and successfully retrieved on Day 2 (M=2.05; SE = 0.21) compared to uncued associations (M ± SE = 1.14 ± 0.15; F(1,58) = 143.51, p<0.001, η2=0.29; Figure 4; see Appendix 1—table 1), in line with the established testing effect (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006; Karpicke and Roediger, 2008), and confirming the efficacy of the selective, association-specific cueing manipulation.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing the testing effect, with reference to Figure 4 and citations.

claims.claim: According to both memory reconsolidation and mnemonic interference accounts, drugs should selectively affect subsequent memory for associations cued and reactivated before the effective action of the drugs on Day 2 but not for uncued items.
claims.source: According to both memory reconsolidation and mnemonic interference accounts, drugs should selectively affect subsequent memory for associations cued and reactivated before the effective action of the drugs on Day 2 but not for uncued items.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on reconsolidation and interference theories.

claims.claim: When collapsing across all cued associations, there was neither a significant Cued × Group interaction nor a main effect of Group on Day 3 associative d' scores.
claims.source: When collapsing across all cued associations (i.e. not considering whether the memory was indeed reactivated), a mixed-design ANOVA on associative d' scores revealed neither a significant Cued × Group interaction nor a main effect of Group (all Fs <2.08, all Ps>0.134), suggesting that the mere presentation of the word cue on Day 2 was insufficient to induce post-retrieval stress hormone effects that change future memory performance.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no overall group effect when not considering reactivation strength.

claims.claim: The mere presentation of the word cue on Day 2 was insufficient to induce post-retrieval stress hormone effects that change future memory performance.
claims.source: When collapsing across all cued associations (i.e. not considering whether the memory was indeed reactivated), a mixed-design ANOVA on associative d' scores revealed neither a significant Cued × Group interaction nor a main effect of Group (all Fs <2.08, all Ps>0.134), suggesting that the mere presentation of the word cue on Day 2 was insufficient to induce post-retrieval stress hormone effects that change future memory performance.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on the statistical result showing no group effect.

claims.claim: Univariate analyses showed no Cued × Group interactions in whole-brain or ROI activity on Day 3.
claims.source: Furthermore, univariate analyses showed no Cued × Group interactions in whole-brain or ROI activity.
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI result showing no group differences in brain activity on Day 3.

claims.claim: Overall, univariate activity on cued and correct trials (Day 2 associative hits) in the hippocampus, PCC, and VTC did not reveal any interaction with Group on subsequent memory (Day 3 associative d').
claims.source: Overall, univariate activity on cued and correct trials (Day 2 associative hits) in the hippocampus, PCC, and VTC did not reveal any interaction with Group on subsequent memory (Day 3 associative d'), suggesting that the average activation across trials and voxels within a single brain area may not suffice to predict post-retrieval effects of noradrenaline or cortisol (all interaction PCorr >0.711).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group interaction with average ROI activity.

claims.claim: The relationship between Day 2 reactivation (indexed by reaction time) and the probability of an associative hit on Day 3 varied across groups.
claims.source: A GLMM was employed to predict associative category hits on Day 3 by Group and Day 2 Reaction time (short, long). A significant interaction (Group × Reaction time (Day 2) interaction: β=0.79 ± 0.30, z=2.61, p=0.008, R2conditional = 0.27; Figure 5A) revealed that the relationship between Day 2 reactivation and the probability of an associative hit on Day 3 varied across groups.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from GLMM analysis, with reference to Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Post-retrieval adrenergic activation (YOH group) differentially impaired subsequent memory following high confidence Day 2 retrieval.
claims.source: Post-hoc marginal means tests revealed a differential decrease in the probability of associative hits on Day 3 in light of short Day 2 reaction times when comparing YOH vs. CORT (β=2.55 ± 0.94, z-ratio=2.55, PCorr = 0.031) and YOH vs. PLAC (β=0.34 ± 0.14, z-ratio=–2.55, PCorr = 0.032).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests showing YOH-specific effects.

claims.claim: Comparing CORT vs. PLAC revealed no difference in the relationship between Day 2 reaction time and Day 3 memory.
claims.source: By contrast, comparing CORT vs. PLAC revealed no such difference (β=0.88 ± 0.37, z-ratio=–0.29, PCorr = 1), suggesting that noradrenergic arousal specifically interacts with strongly reactivated representations after retrieval.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests showing no CORT effect.

claims.claim: Noradrenergic arousal specifically interacts with strongly reactivated representations after retrieval.
claims.source: By contrast, comparing CORT vs. PLAC revealed no such difference (β=0.88 ± 0.37, z-ratio=–0.29, PCorr = 1), suggesting that noradrenergic arousal specifically interacts with strongly reactivated representations after retrieval.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on the pattern of statistical results.

claims.claim: Shorter reaction times and stronger hippocampal activity on Day 2 predicted an increased probability of an associative category hit on Day 3 in the PLAC group.
claims.source: Strikingly, shorter reaction times and stronger hippocampal activity on Day 2 predicted an increased probability of an associative category hit on Day 3 memory in the PLAC group, whereas these measures of stronger reactivation on Day 2 predicted a lower probability of an associative category hit on Day 3 in the YOH group (Group × Hippocampal activity (Day 2) × Reaction time (Day 2) interaction: β=0.90 ± 0.36, z=2.45, PCorr = 0.038, R2conditional = 0.27) but not in the CORT group (β=0.89 ± 0.39, z=2.28, PCorr = 0.068).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from GLMM analysis showing opposite effects in PLAC vs. YOH groups.

claims.claim: Measures of stronger reactivation on Day 2 (shorter reaction times and stronger hippocampal activity) predicted a lower probability of an associative category hit on Day 3 in the YOH group.
claims.source: Strikingly, shorter reaction times and stronger hippocampal activity on Day 2 predicted an increased probability of an associative category hit on Day 3 memory in the PLAC group, whereas these measures of stronger reactivation on Day 2 predicted a lower probability of an associative category hit on Day 3 in the YOH group (Group × Hippocampal activity (Day 2) × Reaction time (Day 2) interaction: β=0.90 ± 0.36, z=2.45, PCorr = 0.038, R2conditional = 0.27) but not in the CORT group (β=0.89 ± 0.39, z=2.28, PCorr = 0.068).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from GLMM analysis showing YOH-specific impairment.

claims.claim: Post-hoc comparisons confirmed significant differences in strongly reinstated trials between YOH and PLAC groups and between YOH and CORT groups, but not between PLAC and CORT groups.
claims.source: Post-hoc comparisons confirmed significant differences in strongly reinstated trials between YOH and PLAC groups (β=–1.12 ± 0.35, z-ratio=–3.13, PCorr = 0.005) and between YOH and CORT groups (β=0.88 ± 0.34, z-ratio=2.58, PCorr = 0.029), but not between PLAC and CORT groups (β=–0.23 ± 0.36, z-ratio=–0.63, PCorr = 1; Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests, with reference to Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Cued memories specifically accompanied by left hippocampal reactivation during Day 2 were associated with increased vulnerability to the influence of post-retrieval YOH.
claims.source: Parallel models with univariate PCC and right hippocampal activity did not yield a significant interaction with Group (all Ps>0.081), suggesting that cued memories specifically accompanied by left hippocampal reactivation during Day 2 was associated with increased vulnerability to the influence of post-retrieval YOH, disrupting post-retrieval processing and subsequent memory on Day 3.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on the pattern of statistical results showing specificity to left hippocampus.

claims.claim: The strength of memory trace reinstatement in the hippocampus, VTC, and PCC during successful memory cueing (Day 2) did not predict the impact of post-retrieval noradrenergic and glucocorticoid activation on subsequent memory (Day 3).
claims.source: We, therefore, tested whether the strength of memory trace reinstatement in the hippocampus, VTC, and PCC during successful memory cueing (Day 2) predicted the impact of post-retrieval noradrenergic and glucocorticoid activation on subsequent memory (Day 3). In contrast to our prediction, none of these regions showed a significant effect that included the factor Group (all PCorr >0.257).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no interaction with event-level reinstatement.

claims.claim: The previously observed post-retrieval noradrenergic subsequent memory impairment may be associated with retrieval-related univariate activity but not the reinstatement of encoding-related neural patterns.
claims.source: These results suggest that the previously observed post-retrieval noradrenergic subsequent memory impairment may be associated with retrieval-related univariate activity but not the reinstatement of encoding-related neural patterns.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on the pattern of results showing effects with univariate activity but not pattern reinstatement.

claims.claim: Reactivation strength (uncued, low VTC reinstatement, high VTC reinstatement) interacted with Group and Hippocampal activity (Day 2) to predict Day 3 memory performance.
claims.source: Testing whether Reactivation strength (uncued, low VTC reinstatement, high VTC reinstatement) interacted with Group and Hippocampal activity (Day 2) to predict Day 3 (24-hr-delayed) memory performance yielded a significant interaction (β=–0.21 ± 0.07, z=–3.08, p=0.002, R2conditional = 0.18; Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from GLMM analysis, with reference to Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Noradrenergic activation significantly affected Day 3 memory for trials associated with stronger trial-wise VTC category-level pattern reinstatement and hippocampal univariate activity on Day 2, resulting in an impairment of subsequent retrieval on Day 3.
claims.source: Post-hoc slope tests confirmed that noradrenergic activation significantly affected Day 3 memory for the trials associated with stronger trial-wise VTC category-level pattern reinstatement and hippocampal univariate activity on Day 2, resulting in an impairment of subsequent retrieval on Day 3 (YOH vs. PLAC: β=0.14 ± 0.05, z-ratio=2.57, PCorr = 0.030; YOH vs. CORT: β=0.13 ± 0.05, z-ratio=1.31, PCorr = 0.708; Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests, with reference to Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Neither drug affected Day 3 memory for trials associated with weaker trial-wise VTC category-level pattern reinstatement and hippocampal univariate activity on Day 2.
claims.source: By contrast, neither drug affected Day 3 memory for the trials associated with weaker trial-wise VTC category-level pattern reinstatement and hippocampal univariate activity on Day 2 (all Ps>0.210).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no drug effect on weakly reactivated trials.

claims.claim: Only the YOH group showed a significant decrease in Day 3 performance when directly comparing the slopes of weak and strong category-level VTC reinstatement in interaction with hippocampal activity.
claims.source: Notably, when directly comparing the slopes of weak and strong category-level VTC reinstatement in interaction with hippocampal activity, only the YOH group showed a significant decrease related to Day 3 performance (YOH: β=0.12 ± 0.05, z-ratio=2.72, PCorr = 0.018; CORT: β = - 0.02±0.05, z-ratio=–0.42, PCorr = 1; PLAC: β = - 0.09±0.05, z-ratio=–1.68, PCorr = 0.274).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from slope comparisons showing YOH-specific effects.

claims.claim: Individual (baseline-to-peak) differences in salivary cortisol and systolic blood pressure did not significantly mediate the observed memory effects.
claims.source: As individual factors, such as metabolism or body weight, can influence the drug's action, we ran an additional analysis in which we included individual (baseline-to-peak) differences in salivary cortisol and (systolic) blood pressure, respectively. This analysis did not show any group by baseline-to-peak difference interaction suggesting that the observed memory effects were mainly driven by the pharmacological intervention group per se and less by individual variation in responses to the drug (see Appendix Inter-individual differences in pharmacological responses did not significantly mediate subsequent memory).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from additional analyses controlling for individual differences.

claims.claim: Predicting Day 3 memory performance by Group and single trial beta activity during memory cueing in the PCC did not reveal a significant interaction.
claims.source: Beyond hippocampal and VTC activity during memory cueing (Day 2), we exploratively reanalysed the GLMMs predicting Day 3 memory performance including the PCC, which was relevant during memory cueing in the current study and in our previous work (Heinbockel et al., 2024). Predicting Day 3 memory performance by the factors Group and Single trial beta activity during memory cueing in the PCC did not reveal a significant interaction (PCorr = 1); adding the factor Reaction time to the model also did not result in a significant interaction (PCorr = 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from exploratory analyses showing no PCC effect.

claims.claim: Predicting Day 3 memory performance by Group and single trial beta activity during memory cueing in the MPFC did not reveal a significant interaction.
claims.source: We also included the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) to predict Day 3 memory performance, as the MPFC has been shown to be sensitive to noradrenergic modulation in previous work (Radley et al., 2008). Predicting Day 3 memory performance by the factors Group and Single trial beta activity during memory cueing in the MPFC did not reveal a significant interaction (PCorr = 1); adding the factor Reaction time to the model also did not result in a significant interaction (PCorr = 1), which indicates that the MPFC was not modulated by either pharmacological intervention.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from exploratory analyses showing no MPFC effect.

claims.claim: Investigating memory cueing from all remaining ROIs that were significantly activated during the Day 2 memory cueing task did not reveal any significant interaction effect with Group on Day 3 memory performance.
claims.source: Finally, we investigated memory cueing from all remaining ROIs that were significantly activated during the Day 2 memory cueing task (Day 2 whole-brain analysis; correct-incorrect; Appendix 1—table 3). We again fit GLMMs predicting Day 3 memory performance by the factors Group and Single trial beta activity during memory cueing. Again, we did not observe any significant interaction effect on any of the ROIs (all interaction PCorr >0.060) and these results did not change when adding the factor Reaction time to the respective models (all PCorr >0.075).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from exploratory analyses of additional ROIs.

claims.claim: Successful cueing was accompanied by significant functional connectivity between the left hippocampus, VTC, PCC, and MPFC.
claims.source: We conducted general psycho-physiological interaction analysis (gPPI) analyses on the Day 2 memory cueing task (remembered – forgotten), which revealed that successful cueing was accompanied by significant functional connectivity between the left hippocampus, VTC, PCC, and MPFC (see Appendix 1—table 4).
claims.evidence: This is a result from gPPI connectivity analysis.

claims.claim: Using connectivity estimates to predict Day 3 subsequent memory performance did not reveal any significant Group × Connectivity interactions.
claims.source: However, using these connectivity estimates to predict Day 3 subsequent memory performance (dprime) via regression did not reveal any significant Group × Connectivity interactions, indicating that the pharmacological manipulation (i.e. noradrenergic stimulation) did not modulate subsequent memory based on functional connectivity during memory cueing (all PCorr >0.228).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group interaction with connectivity.

claims.claim: Including single-trial beta estimates from multiple ROIs during memory cueing to predict Day 3 memory did not reveal any significant interaction effects with Group.
claims.source: The same pattern of results was observed when including single-trial beta estimates from multiple ROIs during memory cueing to predict Day 3 memory (all interaction effects PCorr >0.288).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from additional analyses.

claims.claim: Neural representations from the Memory Cueing task were reinstated significantly offline (i.e. post >pre resting state) in the hippocampus, PCC, and VTC.
claims.source: Aside from examining neural activity related to retrieval during the Memory Cueing task, we also investigated offline reactivation, which is manifested in neural reinstatement observed during the resting-state scans conducted both pre and post-memory cueing (Appendix Tracking offline reactivation). Neural representations from the Memory Cueing task were reinstated significantly offline (i.e. post >pre resting state) in the hippocampus, PCC, and VTC.
claims.evidence: This is a result from offline reactivation analyses described in the appendix.

claims.claim: The initial patterns from encoding were reinstated offline in the VTC.
claims.source: Moreover, the initial patterns from encoding were reinstated offline in the VTC (Appendix Offline encoding and cueing reinstatement in hippocampus and cortical areas).
claims.evidence: This is a result from offline reactivation analyses described in the appendix.

claims.claim: None of the offline reactivation factors interacted with Group when considering Day 3 subsequent memory performance.
claims.source: However, in contrast to the above-reported online reactivation × drug effects, none of these factors interacted with the Group when considering Day 3 subsequent memory performance (Appendix Day 3 offline pattern reactivation does not modulate effects of post-retrieval noradrenergic activation on subsequent memory performance).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result showing no group interaction with offline reactivation.

claims.claim: Post-retrieval noradrenergic activation led to an impairment in subsequent memory, depending on memory strength/confidence, hippocampal activation, and VTC pattern reinstatement during memory reactivation.
claims.source: Our results revealed that post-retrieval noradrenergic activation led to an impairment in subsequent memory, depending on memory strength/confidence, hippocampal activation, and VTC pattern reinstatement during memory reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claims.claim: Post-retrieval glucocorticoid activation did not influence subsequent memory in any way.
claims.source: By contrast, post-retrieval glucocorticoid activation did not influence subsequent memory in any way.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings regarding hydrocortisone.

claims.claim: Previous research showed that administering the beta-blocker propranolol after memory reactivation reduces subsequent memory, potentially interfering with the putative reconsolidation process.
claims.source: Previous research showed that administering the beta-blocker propranolol after memory reactivation reduces subsequent memory, potentially interfering with the putative reconsolidation process (Kindt et al., 2009; Schramm et al., 2016; Przybyslawski et al., 1999; Schwabe et al., 2012a).
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes previous research and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The impairing influence of propranolol on post-retrieval memory has not been consistently replicated.
claims.source: While this impairing influence has not been consistently replicated (Bos et al., 2014b; Elsey et al., 2020; Wood et al., 2015; Muravieva and Alberini, 2010), these results suggest that post-retrieval noradrenaline may facilitate subsequent remembering.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing inconsistent effects.

claims.claim: Increased noradrenergic stimulation after memory retrieval impairs subsequent memory.
claims.source: In contrast to this idea, our results demonstrate that increased noradrenergic stimulation after memory retrieval impairs subsequent memory.
claims.evidence: This is a main finding of the current study.

claims.claim: A key distinction between the current study and prior research using propranolol lies in the emotional nature of the memory task.
claims.source: However, a key distinction between our study and prior research using propranolol lies in the emotional nature of the memory task.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between the current study and previous research.

claims.claim: Previous studies using propranolol predominantly focused on emotionally arousing information or fear memories.
claims.source: Previous studies predominantly focused on emotionally arousing information or fear memories (Lee et al., 2006; Debiec and Ledoux, 2004; Phelps et al., 2004), assuming that post-retrieval propranolol may weaken reconsolidation by attenuating the emotional salience of memories, making them more comparable to neutral ones (Schwabe et al., 2012b).
claims.evidence: This claim describes previous research and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The current study employed emotionally neutral scene images.
claims.source: In our study, we employed emotionally neutral scene images, offering a novel context to explore noradrenergic effects on memory (re)consolidation or mnemonic interference.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the current study.

claims.claim: There may be an inverted u-shaped relationship between post-retrieval noradrenergic arousal and subsequent memory.
claims.source: Furthermore, our findings suggest a potential inverted u-shaped relationship between post-retrieval noradrenergic arousal and subsequent memory, where both noradrenergic blockade by propranolol and strong noradrenergic stimulation induced by yohimbine result in a subsequent memory impairment.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to previous research.

claims.claim: This idea of an inverted U-shaped relationship is in line with previous reports of inverted U-shaped relationships between noradrenergic arousal and memory processes.
claims.source: This idea is in line with previous reports of inverted U-shaped relationships between noradrenergic arousal and memory processes (Arnsten, 2011; Hernaus et al., 2017; Birnbaum et al., 1999; Li and Mei, 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The yohimbine-induced memory impairment critically depended on hippocampal reactivation during memory cueing.
claims.source: Most importantly, our results suggest that the yohimbine-induced memory impairment critically depended on hippocampal reactivation during memory cueing.
claims.evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claims.claim: The hippocampus is crucial for episodic memory formation and retrieval and is highly sensitive to noradrenergic modulation.
claims.source: The hippocampus, crucial for episodic memory formation and retrieval, is highly sensitive to noradrenergic modulation, which can impact hippocampal long-term potentiation and depression (Strange et al., 2014; Katsuki et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Excessive noradrenergic activity in the hippocampus may have disrupted neurotransmission.
claims.source: Excessive noradrenergic activity in the hippocampus may further have disrupted neurotransmission (Kim and Kim, 2023; Diamond et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claims.claim: This disruption may have manifested as deficits in consolidating new retrieval-related memory traces or reconsolidating existing memories.
claims.source: This disruption may have manifested as deficits in consolidating new retrieval-related memory traces or reconsolidating existing memories.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claims.claim: The subsequent memory impairment in the YOH group was additionally dependent on robust activation of the VTC during memory cueing.
claims.source: Furthermore, the subsequent memory impairment in the YOH group was additionally dependent on robust activation of the VTC during memory cueing.
claims.evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claims.claim: These effects could relate to an impeding of the (re)consolidation of visual memory contents, given the VTC's role in processing complex visual stimuli and encoding categorical information.
claims.source: These effects could relate to an impeding of the (re)consolidation of visual memory contents, given the VTC's role in processing complex visual stimuli and encoding categorical information, such as scenes (Bracci et al., 2017; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations about VTC function.

claims.claim: Acute stress is accompanied by a significant increase in cortisol levels, which has been associated with impairments in putative memory reconsolidation after retrieval.
claims.source: In addition to noradrenergic activation, acute stress is accompanied by a significant increase in cortisol levels, which has been associated with impairments in putative memory reconsolidation after retrieval (Maroun and Akirav, 2008; Vafaei et al., 2023; Antypa et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Post-retrieval glucocorticoid activation did not influence subsequent memory, as the placebo and cortisol groups performed similarly in the subsequent memory task.
claims.source: Our results revealed that post-retrieval glucocorticoid activation did not influence subsequent memory, as the placebo and cortisol groups performed similarly in the subsequent memory task.
claims.evidence: This is a main finding of the study.

claims.claim: Acute stress triggers a series of neurochemical changes, and noradrenergic and glucocorticoid activation are strongly intertwined.
claims.source: Acute stress triggers a series of neurochemical changes, and it has been shown that noradrenergic and glucocorticoid activation are strongly intertwined.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about stress physiology based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: The effects of glucocorticoids on memory processes are particularly pronounced when accompanied by high noradrenergic arousal.
claims.source: Accordingly, previous studies have highlighted that the effects of glucocorticoids on memory processes are particularly pronounced when accompanied by high noradrenergic arousal, commonly observed during stressful situations (Schwabe et al., 2022; Roozendaal et al., 2006a; de Quervain et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: In the current study, the administration of hydrocortisone was not associated with an increase in arousal or negative mood.
claims.source: Notably, in the current study, the administration of hydrocortisone was not associated with an increase in arousal or negative mood.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the physiological and mood measurements.

claims.claim: The findings may imply that cortisol alone is not sufficient to influence post-retrieval updating and necessitates concurrent noradrenergic arousal for its memory-modulating effects to fully manifest.
claims.source: As such, our findings may imply that cortisol alone is not sufficient to influence post-retrieval updating and necessitates concurrent noradrenergic arousal for its memory-modulating effects to fully manifest (Maroun and Akirav, 2008; Roozendaal et al., 2006b).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations.

claims.claim: There is evidence suggesting that memory updating depends not only on neural processes during retrieval (i.e. online processing) but also on offline neural reinstatement or replay during post-retrieval rest.
claims.source: There is evidence suggesting that memory updating depends not only on neural processes during retrieval (i.e. online processing) but also on offline neural reinstatement or replay during post-retrieval rest (Staresina et al., 2013; Schlichting and Preston, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The current study tested for the first time whether post-retrieval manipulations of memory are dependent on neural offline reinstatement after memory cueing.
claims.source: Here, we tested for the first time whether post-retrieval manipulations of memory are dependent on neural offline reinstatement after memory cueing.
claims.evidence: This describes a novel aspect of the current study.

claims.claim: The study generally observed significant offline reactivation events in the post-cueing interval compared to pre-cueing.
claims.source: While we generally observed significant offline reactivation events in the post-cueing interval compared to pre-cueing (see Appendix Offline encoding and cueing reinstatement in hippocampus and cortical areas), our findings revealed that neither drug significantly affected subsequent memory via interacting with offline reinstatement dynamics (see Appendix Day 3 offline pattern reactivation does not modulate effects of post-retrieval noradrenergic activation on subsequent memory performance).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the offline reactivation analyses.

claims.claim: Neither drug significantly affected subsequent memory via interacting with offline reinstatement dynamics.
claims.source: While we generally observed significant offline reactivation events in the post-cueing interval compared to pre-cueing (see Appendix Offline encoding and cueing reinstatement in hippocampus and cortical areas), our findings revealed that neither drug significantly affected subsequent memory via interacting with offline reinstatement dynamics (see Appendix Day 3 offline pattern reactivation does not modulate effects of post-retrieval noradrenergic activation on subsequent memory performance).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the offline reactivation analyses.

claims.claim: Offline reinstatement reflects a mere repetition of the neural signal reactivated during retrieval, but these two parameters are not directly comparable.
claims.source: To explain this absence of an effect, it is important to note the differences between the estimated neural online compared to offline parameters. While it might seem that offline reinstatement reflects a mere repetition of the neural signal reactivated during retrieval, these two parameters are not directly comparable.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the lack of offline effects.

claims.claim: The reaction time (confidence) during memory cueing was the most powerful predictor of post-retrieval effects.
claims.source: Finally, on that matter is important to note that the reaction time (confidence) during memory cueing was the most powerful predictor of post-retrieval effects; a predictor that can not be derived from resting state intervals.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the relative importance of different predictors.

claims.claim: In line with the central tenets of reconsolidation theory, the disruptive effects of YOH were contingent on memory reactivation.
claims.source: In line with the central tenets of reconsolidation theory (Nader and Einarsson, 2010; Lee et al., 2017; Schwabe et al., 2014), the disruptive effects of YOH were contingent on memory reactivation.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by the data and citations to reconsolidation theory.

claims.claim: There were no differential effects of noradrenergic activation on cued but incorrectly recalled events relative to uncued events.
claims.source: There were no differential effects of noradrenergic activation on cued but incorrectly recalled events relative to uncued events, suggesting that memories, if not correctly recalled, remained resistant to modification.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claims.claim: Memories, if not correctly recalled, remained resistant to modification.
claims.source: There were no differential effects of noradrenergic activation on cued but incorrectly recalled events relative to uncued events, suggesting that memories, if not correctly recalled, remained resistant to modification.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding.

claims.claim: The extent of neural reactivation on Day 2 correlated with subsequent memory performance.
claims.source: Moreover, the extent of neural reactivation on Day 2 correlated with subsequent memory performance, further underlining the crucial role of neural memory reactivation for post-retrieval modifications of memory.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claims.claim: The triggering of putative reconsolidation is posited to be initiated by prediction errors (PEs).
claims.source: Notably, the triggering of putative reconsolidation is posited to be initiated by prediction errors (PEs; Diaz-Mataix et al., 2013; Sevenster et al., 2013; Fernández et al., 2016).
